title: Interventional Neuropsychiatry and Neuromodulation Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (institution-specific post-residency track; ACGME accreditation not confirmed)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate self-study for physicians who have completed psychiatry residency or are otherwise appropriately trained physicians; MGH states post-residency. This is an educational level only, not admission eligibility.
knowledge: psychiatric diagnostic formulation and risk assessment
prerequisites.technicalPrerequisites: None; no hands-on treatment, device operation, prescribing, or procedural training is provided.
prerequisites.notice: Non-physician learners may use introductory readings, but the curriculum does not qualify any learner to deliver clinical care.

objectives: Integrate psychiatric diagnosis, neurobiological hypotheses, urgency and patient goals into cautious modality discussions.
Distinguish TMS, ECT, ketamine/esketamine, DBS/VNS and emerging approaches by evidence, labeling and clinical context.
Identify referral, consent, safety and monitoring issues for multidisciplinary care.
Critically appraise a device claim, trial or talk for population, protocol, outcomes, generalizability and conflicts.
Accurately state the limits of this independent educational product and of any board or accreditation claims.

units.title: Scope, evidence literacy, and professional role
objectives: Distinguish a clinical institutional fellowship from residency, a combined programme, non-physician credential, research postdoc, and ABMS-recognized specialty/subspecialty.
Separate device class, FDA clearance/approval or HDE, guideline strength, payer coverage, and individual clinical indication.
Identify conflicts and overclaiming in a neuromodulation evidence source.
topics: Interventional psychiatry as cross-modal clinical track; limits of self-study
Randomized trials, pragmatic evidence, external validity, device-label vs protocol distinction
Board/certification and clinical-regulatory scope
boardDomains: ABPN Psychiatry: clinical reasoning and evidence appraisal (adjacent core-domain mapping; not a published fellowship blueprint)
units.casePractice: Classify five fictional programme descriptions as physician fellowship, combined pathway, research/non-physician role, board certificate, or generic category. Explain evidence limits.
units.assessment: One-page evidence-status map. Rubric: 40% correct credential taxonomy, 30% source hierarchy, 20% current-date qualification, 10% explicit uncertainty.

units.title: Circuit neuroscience and formulation
objectives: Describe a clinically useful network/circuit model without treating it as a definitive individual diagnosis.
Relate stimulation target and parameter choices to candidate circuits while distinguishing mechanistic hypotheses from established outcome evidence.
Construct a biopsychosocial and neurological differential before modality selection.
topics: Cortical/subcortical network organization; frontolimbic, salience, default-mode and CSTC concepts
Circuit formulation alongside DSM symptom formulation
Neuroimaging and connectivity: limits, reproducibility, and target uncertainty
boardDomains: Psychiatric diagnosis; neuroscience; evaluation of evidence (course domains, not formal board blueprint)
units.casePractice: Fictional patient with severe depression and comorbid anxiety: write dual diagnosis/circuit formulations and name what cannot be inferred from a group-average circuit model.
units.assessment: Annotated circuit map with three uncertainty statements. Rubric: 35% anatomy/network accuracy, 35% clinical formulation, 20% uncertainty, 10% clarity.

units.title: Candidate assessment, urgency, consent, and shared decisions
objectives: Build a structured assessment covering diagnosis, prior treatment, acuity, capacity, safety, goals, comorbidity, medical risk, and preferences.
Recognize when immediate emergency evaluation/hospitalization supersedes elective neuromodulation referral.
Explain informed consent as individualized, revisited decision-making rather than a generic device form.
topics: MDD/TRD, bipolarity, psychosis, catatonia, substance use, neurocognitive and medical differentials
Suicide-risk assessment, urgent care and safety planning boundaries
Capacity, supported decision making, alternatives, values, and documentation
boardDomains: Psychiatric evaluation; risk assessment; communication and ethics (educational domains, not certification blueprint)
units.casePractice: Fictional high-risk case: produce a referral decision tree and identify red flags for urgent in-person emergency care; do not prescribe a modality or treatment.
units.assessment: Structured consult note. Rubric: 30% safety/urgency, 25% diagnostic formulation, 20% consent/preferences, 15% alternatives, 10% documentation.

units.title: TMS mechanisms, systems, and protocol literacy
objectives: Explain electromagnetic induction and the distinction between a stimulation tool and a treatment protocol.
Compare basic distinctions among conventional rTMS, theta-burst and accelerated schedules without equating them.
Interpret device labeling as device- and indication-specific.
topics: Coils, induced electric field, motor threshold conceptually, target/position reproducibility
Frequency, train structure, intensity, treatment schedule, and personalization as conceptual variables
FDA-cleared protocols and the difference between clearance and blanket clinical recommendation
boardDomains: Treatment mechanisms; clinical pharmacology/therapeutics; interpretation of device evidence (course domains)
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional TMS protocol abstracts and label populations, comparator, endpoints, device, and generalizability; do not recreate an operator workflow.
units.assessment: Evidence table. Rubric: 35% correct protocol taxonomy, 35% evidence interpretation, 20% label distinctions, 10% caveats.

units.title: TMS safety, screening, monitoring, and referral
objectives: Identify material questions about metallic/electronic implants, seizure risk, medications and changing clinical state that require device-specific professional review.
Explain why TMS is not a response to an acute psychiatric emergency and why symptom worsening needs escalation.
Use a referral checklist without claiming it confers authority to administer treatment.
topics: Screening categories and manufacturer IFU/device-specific compatibility
Seizure risk and emergency readiness; suicidality/clinical worsening monitoring
Informed referral, accessibility, follow-up, and quality monitoring
boardDomains: Patient safety; systems-based practice; adverse effects and risk management (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional consultation with a remote head implant and remote seizure: formulate questions for the treating/device team; do not make a clearance determination.
units.assessment: Safety referral memo. Rubric: 40% recognizes stop-and-consult signals, 25% no unsupported yes/no safety clearance, 20% urgency plan, 15% communication.

units.title: ECT: indications, technique trade-offs, and cognitive outcomes
objectives: Recognize evidence-supported clinical contexts for considering ECT, including urgent severe illness, while avoiding simplistic treatment-line rules.
Summarize how electrode placement and pulse characteristics create efficacy/cognition trade-offs at a conceptual level.
Plan shared review of cognitive effects and individualized response tracking.
topics: ECT in severe depression, mania/psychosis and catatonia; urgency and local law
Anesthesia, seizure physiology and multidisciplinary care at a conceptual level
Placement/pulse-width trade-offs, cognitive monitoring, relapse/continuation concepts
boardDomains: Mood and psychotic disorders; catatonia; therapeutics; adverse effects (course domains)
units.casePractice: Use the linked report of ECT with an implanted sacral neuromodulator as a question-generation exercise only; inspect original clinician/device team reasoning and limitations; do not copy images or patient information.
units.assessment: Case conference memo. Rubric: 30% indication/risk framing, 25% consent/cognition, 25% multidisciplinary coordination, 20% evidence limits.

units.title: ECT safety, consent, anesthesia interface, and continuity
objectives: Describe which team roles and safety systems are essential around ECT without performing or directing the procedure.
Identify capacity, assent/representative, legal and jurisdiction-specific issues for consent.
Distinguish acute-course response from continuation/maintenance planning and transitions of care.
topics: Pre-treatment assessment and anesthesia consultation
Consent, capacity, legal safeguards, and patient/caregiver communication
Post-course monitoring, cognition, relapse prevention and coordination
boardDomains: Ethics and professionalism; safety; continuity of care (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional case where cognition changes during ECT: write questions and escalation pathways for the multidisciplinary team.
units.assessment: Shared-decision checklist. Rubric: 30% rights/capacity, 30% risk communication, 20% continuity, 20% role boundaries.

units.title: Ketamine and esketamine: pharmacology, regulation, and care model
objectives: Distinguish racemic ketamine, esketamine, route, product labeling and evidence bases.
Apply current SPRAVATO label warnings, indication limits, monitoring and REMS boundaries in an educational case.
Identify misuse, substance use, dissociation, cardiovascular and respiratory risks and the need for qualified in-person care.
topics: NMDA/glutamate hypotheses; rapid antidepressant evidence and uncertainty
Esketamine label indication, supervision/REMS, monitoring and limitations
IV/other ketamine uses: not interchangeable with FDA-labeled esketamine; local standard and evidence review
boardDomains: Psychopharmacology; substance use; adverse effects; regulatory literacy (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional outpatient asks whether a consumer at-home ketamine kit is equivalent to labeled esketamine care: identify label/evidence distinctions, risk questions and referral response.
units.assessment: Product/regulatory comparison. Rubric: 40% label accuracy, 25% safety, 20% evidence limits, 15% patient-centered wording.

units.title: Invasive neuromodulation: DBS, VNS, neurosurgery interfaces
objectives: Compare implanted DBS and VNS with noninvasive modalities in broad mechanisms, coordination demands, and device-specific regulatory pathways.
Explain that FDA PMA/HDE status is product-specific and does not equal universal clinical indication or board credential.
Formulate the multidisciplinary questions required before referral.
topics: Device classes and implantable-system care interfaces
Psychiatric DBS evidence, HDE and severe OCD product-specific context
VNS labeling, indications, long-term follow-up and device-programming team roles
boardDomains: Psychiatric therapeutics; neuropsychiatry; systems-based multidisciplinary care (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional patient with severe OCD and an implanted device seeks another intervention; develop an MDT consultation question list, not a candidacy decision.
units.assessment: Multidisciplinary referral map. Rubric: 35% identifies relevant specialties, 30% regulatory precision, 20% longitudinal care, 15% limits.

units.title: tDCS and emerging modalities: evidence maturity and responsible innovation
objectives: Classify tDCS, photobiomodulation and low-intensity focused ultrasound as topics named by the fellowship while separating established clinical use from emerging evidence.
Appraise mechanisms, feasibility and bias in early-stage studies.
Communicate uncertainty without implying clearance, standard-of-care status or equal evidence.
topics: tDCS indications/evidence and jurisdiction/device variation
tPBM and LIFUP: investigational/evolving evidence as listed by official programme
Trial design, sham controls, preregistration, outcomes and device conflicts
boardDomains: Evidence-based practice; research literacy; professionalism (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional clinician encounters a commercial claim for a novel device: produce a dated evidence/label checklist before communicating with a patient.
units.assessment: Two-page evidence appraisal. Rubric: 35% design appraisal, 25% regulatory distinctions, 25% uncertainty, 15% conflict disclosure.

units.title: Longitudinal outcomes, adverse events, relapse prevention, and service design
objectives: Select measurement-based outcomes appropriate to clinical context while acknowledging instrument and follow-up limitations.
Design a continuity map across referring psychiatrist, intervention service, anesthesia/neurosurgery and crisis services.
Discuss access, cost and equity without inferring local availability or benefit.
topics: Symptoms, cognition, function, patient-defined outcomes, adverse effects and follow-up
Maintenance/relapse prevention evidence by modality
Referral access, service quality and continuity
boardDomains: Patient care; quality improvement; health systems; professionalism (course domains)
units.casePractice: Fictional care-transition diagram after acute treatment response with explicit escalation route for deterioration.
units.assessment: Quality-improvement storyboard. Rubric: 30% measures, 30% safety/continuity, 20% patient priorities, 20% feasibility/equity.

units.title: Integrated modality-selection conference and evidence synthesis
objectives: Integrate diagnosis, acuity, prior treatments, evidence, product label, values, risks, alternatives and access into a defensible educational recommendation.
State when evidence is missing, when to defer a decision, and when urgent care is needed.
Separate a training curriculum from accredited supervised training, eligibility and independent clinical competence.
topics: Cross-modality comparative evidence and no universal sequence
Case-conference communication, referral and documented uncertainty
Credential limits and research agenda
boardDomains: Integrated clinical reasoning; ethics; evidence appraisal (course-specific domains, no separate board exam)
units.casePractice: Fictional multidisciplinary conference compares options for three presentations: urgent catatonia, non-emergent TRD, and severe OCD. No treatment order/dose given; articulate why patient-specific specialist assessment is essential.
units.assessment: Capstone oral presentation and 1,000-word evidence brief. Rubric: 30% safety, 25% evidence/labels, 20% patient values, 15% team/referral plan, 10% humility and limits.

questions.stem: An institution advertises a one-year post-residency Interventional Neuropsychiatry and Neuromodulation Fellowship with longitudinal TMS, ECT, ketamine and invasive-neuromodulation clinics. What is the most accurate classification?

options.text: A new ABMS-recognized medical specialty with a guaranteed separate certification examination.
An institution-specific clinical fellowship track spanning several modalities; its listing alone does not establish ACGME accreditation or board eligibility.
A combined Psychiatry/Neurology residency.
A research-only postdoctoral job.

questions.rationale: MGH describes it as a one-year post-residency clinical fellowship and describes longitudinal core clinics and research. ABPN/ABMS lists do not identify an interventional-neuromodulation board subspecialty or separate exam. ACGME/residency rules do not imply this specific fellowship is accredited.

questions.stem: A public TMS lecture transcript is accessible, but the stateless YouTube page does not expose player runtime and the metadata request is met by a bot challenge. What is appropriate in an evidence ledger?

options.text: Estimate duration from transcript word count and count it.
Record runtime as unknown, state what was accessible and do not count the item until runtime is observed.
Use the webinar’s advertised CME duration as exact player length.
Use another video from the same playlist as a proxy.

questions.rationale: The contract requires observed runtimes and prohibits estimates or bypassing login/dynamic barriers. Timestamped transcript proves transcript content, not exact recording runtime.

questions.stem: A TMS referral mentions an electronic implant in or near the head. Which next step best respects FDA device guidance?

options.text: Assume all implants are safe if the patient is asymptomatic.
Check the exact device’s current labeling and compatibility with the treating service/manufacturer; do not make clearance from a generic lecture.
Use the same distance rule for every TMS device without exception.
Proceed because magnetic stimulation does not interact with electronics.

questions.rationale: FDA guidance describes implant and conductive-material compatibility concerns and expects device-specific labeling/screening. A course checklist is not clearance or an operator qualification.

questions.stem: A patient in an educational vignette has catatonia, poor oral intake and rapidly escalating medical risk. Which principle should guide triage?

options.text: Wait for multiple routine outpatient medication failures before urgent consultation.
Urgent in-person psychiatric/medical evaluation is needed; ECT may be considered in appropriate emergency contexts by qualified clinicians, but this module cannot direct treatment.
TMS is a substitute for emergency evaluation.
An online course can select and authorize an ECT procedure.

questions.rationale: The cited ECT guidance describes catatonia, poor intake and high suicidality among potential urgent contexts. Emergency assessment and local clinician judgment remain essential; this is not patient-specific advice.

questions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes FDA labeling for SPRAVATO as of the reviewed March 2026 DailyMed version?

options.text: It is interchangeable with any compounded or IV racemic ketamine treatment.

It is esketamine nasal spray for adult TRD and specified depressive symptoms with acute suicidal ideation/behavior; the label includes supervised administration, REMS and monitoring requirements and does not demonstrate suicide prevention.
It is approved as an anesthetic.
It is approved for pediatric depression.

questions.rationale: The label lists adult indications, supervised administration, blood-pressure monitoring, REMS and at least two-hour observation for specified risks. It says effectiveness in preventing suicide or reducing suicidal ideation/behavior has not been demonstrated and it is not an anesthetic.

questions.stem: A video speaker presents a personally successful TMS case and claims a protocol is appropriate for most patients. What critical-appraisal response is strongest?

options.text: One compelling case establishes general efficacy.
Separate anecdote and disclosure from controlled evidence, label, study population, outcomes and replication; compare the claim with current independent sources.
Industry involvement means all information is false.
A speaker’s board certification proves a protocol is FDA-cleared.

questions.rationale: Clinical content must be triangulated with evidence and product labeling. Conflicts are relevant context, neither automatic proof nor disproof. Clearance and credentials are separate questions.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is justified from the MGH fellowship’s published overview?

options.text: Every fellow receives a stated number of independently verified procedures and passes a board exam.

It describes one-year longitudinal core clinics, weekly hour-long didactics and protected research, but the public overview does not provide a complete public lecture archive or verified procedure counts.
It is an adult-child combined residency.
All sample topics are freely reusable recordings.

questions.rationale: The official page details clinics, didactics, topics and research but does not publish procedure counts or an entire transferable media collection. No invented volume, eligibility or content claims should be added.

questions.stem: A team discusses implanted DBS for severe OCD. What is the safest regulatory interpretation?

options.text: All psychiatric DBS systems are FDA-approved for any mood or anxiety diagnosis.
Check the exact device’s current FDA HDE/label and multidisciplinary criteria; a humanitarian device exemption is device- and indication-specific, not a general psychiatric license.
An HDE means the procedure is a board subspecialty.
DBS needs no neurosurgical follow-up.

questions.rationale: The FDA HDE record is for a specific system and use. Regulatory pathway does not establish universal indication, board certification or competence.

questions.stem: What is an appropriate use of an open published case report about ECT in a patient with an implanted sacral neurostimulator?

options.text: Rehost its image because the article is freely viewable.
Link to the source for critical educational discussion, check the article’s license before reuse, and do not copy patient records or images into this course.
Treat one case as a blanket compatibility rule for all implants.
Assume de-identification means no consent or copyright restrictions apply.

questions.rationale: Free-to-view is not reuse permission; one case cannot replace device-specific team assessment. Article text/image rights and patient protections remain applicable.

questions.stem: A clinician wants to choose between TMS, ECT, ketamine/esketamine, and DBS for an individual with complex depression. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Apply a universal linear sequence based only on the diagnostic label.
Assess diagnosis, acuity, risk, prior care, preferences, comorbidity, evidence, exact product labeling and multidisciplinary options; escalate urgent risks and document uncertainty.
Select the least invasive option regardless of urgency or contraindications.
Infer candidacy from a circuit diagram alone.

questions.rationale: No single modality sequence fits every case; MGH emphasizes individual circuit-based formulation while primary labeling and guidelines require clinical context. Emergency risk takes precedence and specialist evaluation is needed.

unitMap.text: Scope, evidence literacy, and professional role
coveredTopics: Interventional psychiatry as cross-modal clinical track; limits of self-study
Randomized trials, pragmatic evidence, external validity, device-label vs protocol distinction
Board/certification and clinical-regulatory scope

unitMap.text: Circuit neuroscience and formulation
coveredTopics: Cortical/subcortical network organization; frontolimbic, salience, default-mode and CSTC concepts
Circuit formulation alongside DSM symptom formulation
Neuroimaging and connectivity: limits, reproducibility, and target uncertainty

unitMap.text: Candidate assessment, urgency, consent, and shared decisions
coveredTopics: MDD/TRD, bipolarity, psychosis, catatonia, substance use, neurocognitive and medical differentials
Suicide-risk assessment, urgent care and safety planning boundaries
Capacity, supported decision making, alternatives, values, and documentation

unitMap.text: TMS mechanisms, systems, and protocol literacy
coveredTopics: Coils, induced electric field, motor threshold conceptually, target/position reproducibility
Frequency, train structure, intensity, treatment schedule, and personalization as conceptual variables
FDA-cleared protocols and the difference between clearance and blanket clinical recommendation

unitMap.text: TMS safety, screening, monitoring, and referral
coveredTopics: Screening categories and manufacturer IFU/device-specific compatibility
Seizure risk and emergency readiness; suicidality/clinical worsening monitoring
Informed referral, accessibility, follow-up, and quality monitoring

unitMap.text: ECT: indications, technique trade-offs, and cognitive outcomes
coveredTopics: ECT in severe depression, mania/psychosis and catatonia; urgency and local law
Anesthesia, seizure physiology and multidisciplinary care at a conceptual level
Placement/pulse-width trade-offs, cognitive monitoring, relapse/continuation concepts

unitMap.text: ECT safety, consent, anesthesia interface, and continuity
coveredTopics: Pre-treatment assessment and anesthesia consultation
Consent, capacity, legal safeguards, and patient/caregiver communication
Post-course monitoring, cognition, relapse prevention and coordination

unitMap.text: Ketamine and esketamine: pharmacology, regulation, and care model
coveredTopics: NMDA/glutamate hypotheses; rapid antidepressant evidence and uncertainty
Esketamine label indication, supervision/REMS, monitoring and limitations
IV/other ketamine uses: not interchangeable with FDA-labeled esketamine; local standard and evidence review

unitMap.text: Invasive neuromodulation: DBS, VNS, neurosurgery interfaces
coveredTopics: Device classes and implantable-system care interfaces
Psychiatric DBS evidence, HDE and severe OCD product-specific context
VNS labeling, indications, long-term follow-up and device-programming team roles

unitMap.text: tDCS and emerging modalities: evidence maturity and responsible innovation
coveredTopics: tDCS indications/evidence and jurisdiction/device variation
tPBM and LIFUP: investigational/evolving evidence as listed by official programme
Trial design, sham controls, preregistration, outcomes and device conflicts

unitMap.text: Longitudinal outcomes, adverse events, relapse prevention, and service design
coveredTopics: Symptoms, cognition, function, patient-defined outcomes, adverse effects and follow-up
Maintenance/relapse prevention evidence by modality
Referral access, service quality and continuity

unitMap.text: Integrated modality-selection conference and evidence synthesis
coveredTopics: Cross-modality comparative evidence and no universal sequence
Case-conference communication, referral and documented uncertainty
Credential limits and research agenda

topicGaps: All eight candidate recordings (four pre-existing plus four new NIMH lecture links) remain excluded: exact full-player runtimes were not exposed through the accessible public pages; transcript timestamps are not duration evidence. Verified external video time is 0.0 h; target gap remains 36.0 h.

The new NIMH archive provides relevant freely linked TMS didactics in parameters/protocols, physics/devices/modeling, cortical neurophysiology and safety. As archived 2020 materials, they require comparison with current device-specific instructions and cannot serve as an operator course; their exact lengths remain unknown.

No exact public runtime evidence or a complete, freely accessible, verified lecture-series ledger was found for ECT cognitive/maintenance practice, ketamine/esketamine service models, psychiatric DBS/VNS, tDCS/tPBM/LIFUP, longitudinal outcomes, or the MGH fellowship's didactic archive.

Current and specialty-specific sources remain needed for modality-specific clinical decisions, developmental/older-adult use, and evolving product indications; any dated regulatory statement must be checked against the current device label and applicable jurisdiction.

Publicly accessible didactic recordings do not provide supervised practice, institutional procedure volumes, eligibility, accreditation, licensure or board certification. The named fellowship has no separate board examination identified; parent ABPN Psychiatry domains are adjacent only, not a fellowship blueprint.

topicGaps: All eight candidate recordings (four pre-existing plus four new NIMH lecture links) remain excluded: exact full-player runtimes were not exposed through the accessible public pages; transcript timestamps are not duration evidence. Verified external video time is 0.0 h; target gap remains 36.0 h.

The new NIMH archive provides relevant freely linked TMS didactics in parameters/protocols, physics/devices/modeling, cortical neurophysiology and safety. As archived 2020 materials, they require comparison with current device-specific instructions and cannot serve as an operator course; their exact lengths remain unknown.

No exact public runtime evidence or a complete, freely accessible, verified lecture-series ledger was found for ECT cognitive/maintenance practice, ketamine/esketamine service models, psychiatric DBS/VNS, tDCS/tPBM/LIFUP, longitudinal outcomes, or the MGH fellowship's didactic archive.

Current and specialty-specific sources remain needed for modality-specific clinical decisions, developmental/older-adult use, and evolving product indications; any dated regulatory statement must be checked against the current device label and applicable jurisdiction.

Publicly accessible didactic recordings do not provide supervised practice, institutional procedure volumes, eligibility, accreditation, licensure or board certification. The named fellowship has no separate board examination identified; parent ABPN Psychiatry domains are adjacent only, not a fellowship blueprint.

title: Forensic Psychiatry Fellowship
prerequisites: For licensed psychiatrists or psychiatry residents/advanced learners studying under supervision; foundational psychiatry and diagnostic reasoning.
Working knowledge of U.S. civil/criminal procedure and legal research; laws vary by jurisdiction, so each assignment begins with jurisdiction identification.
No procedural, prescribing, testimony, evaluation-service, licensure, or board-certification permission is granted.
objectives: Distinguish forensic and treatment roles and make impartial, scope-limited conclusions.
Translate a legally defined referral question into a transparent evidence plan.
Integrate records, interviews, collateral data and appropriate tests with alternative explanations and uncertainty.
Map opinions to current legal tests without treating psychiatric diagnosis as a legal conclusion.
Communicate defensible findings in reports and testimony while recognizing professional, ethical, cultural, and systems limitations.
Map study to the ABPN forensic psychiatry exam blueprint and verify current rules/standards independently.

units.title: Foundations: role, referral question, and forensic-clinical boundary
objectives: Distinguish treatment from evaluation and define the retaining question, role, jurisdiction, and limits before accepting a referral.
Use impartiality, informed participation, confidentiality limits, and competence boundaries to plan an evaluation.
topics: Forensic role and ethics
Referral scope and conflicts
Interdisciplinary interface
units.casePractice: Use only linked, published/legal case resources and fictionalized course scenarios. Do not copy patient records or clinical images. Apply the jurisdiction, role, source-quality, and uncertainty checks in the unit rubric.
units.assessment: Draft a pre-evaluation letter defining role, scope, records requested, limits, and conflicts; peer-score scope, neutrality, and jurisdictional caveats.

units.title: Adjudicative competence and restoration
objectives: Separate the legal functional question from diagnosis and risk; explain Dusky-style understanding and ability to assist counsel while checking local law.
Integrate interview, records, collateral sources, and functional observations; identify restoration and confinement questions as jurisdiction-specific.
topics: Competence to stand trial
Competence to proceed pro se
Restoration and treatment-over-objection standards

units.assessment: Write a structured functional analysis from a fictional vignette; rubric: legal question 25%, data integration 25%, functional nexus 25%, limits/jurisdiction 25%.

units.title: Criminal responsibility and mental state at offense
objectives: Reconstruct mental state at the legally relevant time from contemporaneous and retrospective evidence while stating jurisdictional insanity standards.

topics: Insanity standards vary by jurisdiction

Substance-related defenses and limits
units.casePractice: Use only linked, published/legal case resources and fictionalized course scenarios. Do not copy patient records or clinical images. Apply the jurisdiction, role, source-quality, and uncertainty checks in the unit rubric.
units.assessment: Prepare a two-column evidence map separating clinical findings from legal criteria; rubric: temporal reasoning 30%, differential 25%, source quality 25%, uncertainty 20%.

units.title: Civil commitment, rights, capacity, and guardianship

Rights, confidentiality, privilege, duty to protect
units.casePractice: Use only linked, published/legal case resources and fictionalized course scenarios. Do not copy patient records or clinical images. Apply the jurisdiction, role, source-quality, and uncertainty checks in the unit rubric.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional forensic report portfolio
assignment.instructions: Using only the fictional course vignette supplied by the learner (no real patient records), prepare a referral-scope memo, evidence matrix, structured functional formulation, concise report, and oral-testimony reflection. Choose one jurisdiction and cite current law; do not generate a clinical opinion for an actual case.
assignment.submissionRestrictions: No personal health information, real patient records, identifiable case narrative, or copyrighted exam items.

assessment.plan: 12 formative case analyses, two peer critiques, one integrated fictional report portfolio, and a 10-item original self-check set. Suggested thresholds are course completion criteria only; these items are not validated predictors of ABPN performance or credentialing.
assessment.rubric: Use unit assignment rubrics above. Require citations to applicable current law and source provenance; feedback should separate clinical reasoning, legal standard, and writing.
assessment.boardPreparationNotice: The ABPN content specifications are a planning map, not a complete test blueprint or guarantee of coverage/passing. Questions are original educational items, not official or recalled exam questions.

studyHours.breakdown: 40 verified public lecture hours targeted, plus 40 hours readings and case-law study, 24 hours written/oral assignments, and 16 hours review. Study time is a suggested learner plan, not measured institutional didactic or clinical hours.

mapping.name: Harvard Mass General Brigham Forensic Psychiatry Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page states one-year, full-time ACGME-accredited fellowship at MGH/BWH; supervised criminal and civil evaluations, reports, testimony, correctional-facility treatment, didactics, research, mock testimony. Describes Bridgewater State Hospital (six months), New England Forensic Associates/Institute for Sexual Wellness, BWH Consultation-Liaison service, Boston Juvenile Court Clinic, and MGH Law & Psychiatry Service. These are published rotation summaries, not full syllabus, measured contact hours, volume guarantees, or this course’s placements.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best separates adjudicative competence from diagnosis?

options.text: A psychotic-disorder diagnosis automatically establishes incompetence.
Competence is a jurisdictional functional legal question; diagnosis may be relevant evidence but does not decide it.
Competence is a personality trait measured by one scale.
A treating psychiatrist’s capacity assessment is interchangeable with CST.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The legal question concerns ability to understand proceedings and assist counsel under governing law; diagnosis is not a substitute.

practiceQuestions.stem: A defendant can accurately repeat courtroom vocabulary but cannot rationally discuss evidence or work with counsel because of fixed delusions. What is the strongest next analytic step?

options.text: Conclude competent because vocabulary is intact.
Document only diagnosis.
Assess both understanding and rational/functional ability to consult counsel, with concrete examples and collateral data.
Predict guilt.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The evaluation maps abilities to the legal functional question rather than equating rote knowledge with competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: When reconstructing criminal responsibility at the time of an alleged offense, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Use present diagnosis alone.
Anchor analysis to contemporaneous and collateral evidence, timeline symptoms, and the jurisdiction’s legal test; state uncertainty.
Assume substance use decides responsibility.
Avoid reviewing records because the interview is sufficient.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A retrospective mental-state opinion requires time-specific data and law-specific criteria, with alternative explanations.

practiceQuestions.stem: An evaluee asks whether the forensic interview is confidential like therapy. What should be done?

options.text: Promise absolute confidentiality.
Explain role, recipient, purpose, foreseeable limits, and applicable privilege/reporting rules before substantive interview.
Decline to discuss the referral.
Say confidentiality rules are identical in every state.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Role-appropriate advance explanation and jurisdiction-specific rules protect informed participation and avoid misleading assurances.

practiceQuestions.stem: A risk report states “high risk” but does not specify outcome, time horizon, data, or management scenario. What is the central defect?

options.text: It is too short.
It omits a transparent, contextualized formulation and limits; risk labels are not deterministic.
It should name a diagnosis.
A risk opinion is never permitted.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A useful formulation makes the target, time frame, evidence, context, uncertainty, and management implications explicit.

practiceQuestions.stem: A single elevated validity-scale result is offered as proof that the examinee is malingering. Best response?

options.text: Accept it as diagnostic.
Interpret test validity and context, integrate interview/records/collateral, consider alternatives, and avoid a single-test conclusion.
Disregard all psychological testing.
Use the score to infer criminal intent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Test scores are evidence that require construct-valid interpretation and convergence; no single score resolves the legal question.

practiceQuestions.stem: Under current Federal Rule of Evidence 702, the proponent must show which?

options.text: Only that the witness holds an MD.
More likely than not that the expert will help, has sufficient basis, uses reliable principles/methods and reliably applies them.
That the opinion is certainly correct.
That the court accepts a specific clinical diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Rule 702’s text requires qualification/helpfulness and sufficient basis, reliable method, reliable application under the stated threshold. State rules may differ.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child forensic evaluation may use the same adult interview verbatim if the evaluator is experienced.

options.text: True; age does not affect suggestibility.
False; methods should be developmentally appropriate and minimize suggestion, with jurisdictional referral question defined.
True; caregiver report alone proves the allegation.
False; no youth can participate in forensic interviews.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Development, language, cognitive abilities, and suggestibility affect method; avoid conclusions beyond data.

practiceQuestions.stem: A jail psychiatrist receives a forensic evaluation referral for a patient they currently treat. What is the best initial move?

options.text: Accept without clarification.
Identify conflicts and role expectations, disclose limits, determine whether impartiality and competence can be maintained, and consider referral/consultation.
Provide a legal conclusion through treatment notes.
Stop treatment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Multiple relationships and role confusion may impair objectivity; analyze and communicate the limits before proceeding.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public fellowship page advertises ACGME-accredited training. Does that alone guarantee an individual graduate is board-eligible?

options.text: Yes, always.
No; the ABPN has its own published certification eligibility rules and credentials review.
Only if the fellow passed a mock exam.
Yes, if the trainee completed this independent course.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A training page and ABPN eligibility criteria are different evidence; ABPN states primary psychiatry certification and accredited fellowship training requirements.

title: Addiction Psychiatry Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study curriculum; not a fellowship or training program)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced physician self-study for learners with medical school and psychiatry-residency foundations. Not an entry-to-practice course.
priorKnowledge: Clinical epidemiology, ethics/privacy and team-based care
prerequisites.notice: Non-physicians may use selected conceptual material but must not use this course to diagnose, prescribe, supervise withdrawal, perform procedures or provide care.

objectives: Map Addiction Psychiatry scope and ABPN blueprint without conflating programme accreditation, board certification, Addiction Medicine, research roles or self-study.
Formulate SUD with longitudinal biopsychosocial interview, DSM criteria, differential and testing caveats.
Explain evidence and clinical reasoning for alcohol, opioid, stimulant, tobacco, cannabis and other disorders, withdrawal/intoxication, comorbidity and special populations.
Compare person-centered communication, psychosocial and pharmacologic treatment concepts and care transitions.
Appraise guideline certainty, identify dated claims, respect ethics/privacy and connect to appropriate care systems.

units.title: Addiction science and person-first formulation
objectives: Explain reward, learning, salience, stress and executive-control models without reducing people to disease labels.
Use non-stigmatizing language; distinguish exposure, risky use, use disorder and recovery.
units.casePractice: Formulate two fictional cases biopsychosocially; identify stigmatizing wording.
units.assessment: Concept map; 40% science, 30% person-first language, 30% context.

units.title: Screening, diagnostic interview and DSM-5-TR reasoning
objectives: Take a time-bounded substance history and assess immediate medical/psychiatric safety first.
Apply 11 DSM criteria, severity, remission and differential diagnosis.
Interpret toxicology in context; do not equate test result with diagnosis.

units.casePractice: Fictional interview worksheet: missing data, differential and test limitations.
units.assessment: Formulation: 40% criteria/time course, 35% differential/safety, 25% testing/communication.

units.title: Engagement, motivational interviewing and relationship
objectives: Demonstrate open questions, affirmations, reflections and summaries.
Support autonomy and shared goals without coercion or false binaries.
Plan individual, group, family and community support with consent.
units.casePractice: Role-play fictional patient who wants to cut down; no real patient data.
units.assessment: MI analysis: 35% empathy/autonomy, 30% reflections, 25% collaborative next step, 10% non-stigmatizing language.

units.title: Alcohol-related disorders: diagnosis, course and comorbidity
objectives: Distinguish intoxication, withdrawal, AUD, risky use and medical harm.
Assess severity, psychiatric/cognitive/hepatic/pain and medication factors.
Use NIAAA resource to frame treatment/referral.

units.casePractice: Fictional outpatient formulation; do not diagnose from one lab result.
units.assessment: 35% diagnosis/differential, 35% risk/comorbidity, 30% shared plan.

Compare setting factors conceptually using ASAM guidance.
Explain withdrawal management is not AUD treatment; plan continuity.
units.casePractice: Fictional triage case: red flags and setting questions; no dosing exercise.
units.assessment: 40% urgent signs, 30% setting reasoning, 30% transition.

units.title: Opioid-related disorders, overdose prevention and MOUD

units.casePractice: Fictional post-overdose case: shared-choice menu and safety/continuity checklist; no doses.
units.assessment: 35% evidence/choice, 30% safety, 25% continuity/access, 10% caveats.

units.title: Stimulant use disorder, intoxication, withdrawal and contingency management
objectives: Assess urgent toxicity before longitudinal formulation.

units.casePractice: Fictional case: urgent issues and CM-informed conceptual care plan.
units.assessment: 45% guideline fidelity, 25% triage, 20% co-occurring plan, 10% caveats.

units.title: Pain, prescribed medicines and SUD
objectives: Build a nonjudgmental pain/medicine/substance history.
Differentiate SUD using criteria, not stereotypes or single red flags.
Coordinate pain, psychiatry, primary-care and addiction teams.
units.casePractice: Read published source in place; do not reproduce. Compare with a new fictional composite.
units.assessment: 35% differential, 30% safety/function, 25% coordination, 10% source limits.

units.title: Sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic and other substance disorders
objectives: Identify substance-specific intoxication/withdrawal differentials and polysubstance risk.
Use current labels/guidelines rather than extrapolating from this course.
Frame caffeine, inhalant, hallucinogen, PCP and novel substances clinically.

assignment.title: Fictional integrated case formulation and evidence map
assignment.prompt: Write a 1,200–1,800 word formulation using an invented composite: priorities, use timeline, diagnostic criteria/differential, medical/psychiatric risk questions, options, shared decisions, safety/continuity and evidence map. No patient-specific doses, published-case copying or real patient information.
deliverables: Labeled fictional case
DSM/differential worksheet
Claim/source/qualifier evidence map
Handoff/referral framework
assignment.passCriterion: Formative rubric only; suggested 80% with no critical safety/privacy/scope error. Not competency or board evaluation.

assessment.format: Formative retrieval checks in 12 units, ten original MCQs, source critique and fictional capstone.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated pass score, predictor or official ABPN exam questions.

unitMap.text: Addiction science and person-first formulation
Screening, diagnostic interview and DSM-5-TR reasoning
Engagement, motivational interviewing and relationship
Alcohol-related disorders: diagnosis, course and comorbidity
Alcohol withdrawal and stabilization principles
Opioid-related disorders, overdose prevention and MOUD
Stimulant use disorder, intoxication, withdrawal and contingency management
Pain, prescribed medicines and SUD
Sedative, hypnotic, anxiolytic and other substance disorders
Cannabis, pregnancy, adolescence and special populations
Tobacco use disorder, nicotine and integrated psychiatric care
Co-occurring conditions, gambling, law, systems and lifelong learning

topicGaps: Verified free, observed-duration external runtime is 7.5469 h (27169 s), leaving 28.4531 h below the 36 h floor. The newly appended NIDA video is a single 33:27 COVID-era opioid-safety interview; original episode scripts are not recordings and do not close the runtime gap.

Unfilled or insufficiently taught board-relevant lecture topics remain: alcohol withdrawal/medications; core OUD care; sedatives; caffeine; inhalants; hallucinogens; PCP; gambling; forensic issues; diagnostic testing; family/group psychotherapy; law/ethics/access/QI. Six complete episode scripts (one introductory and five worked examples) add source-backed instruction in formulation, toxicology, alcohol-withdrawal continuity, MOUD reasoning, stimulant care, and benzodiazepine risk, but do not fully close these topic gaps.
Original teaching episodes in the separate authored file are scripted/planned only, not rendered or recorded. Their narration targets do not count toward verified media hours.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) — Addiction Psychiatry subspecialty certification examination

boardStatus.status: ABPN has a distinct Addiction Psychiatry subspecialty certificate and separate initial examination. Not ABPM Addiction Medicine.
boardStatus.blueprint: ABPN 2026 content specifications, posted March 2026; 220 items and two dimensions.
boardStatus.adjacentBoard: ABPM Addiction Medicine is a separate multidisciplinary subspecialty board certification.
boardStatus.halfTimeTrack: MGB reports two-year half-time clinical/research option. ABPN requires one continuous year at no less than half-time; verify individual documentation/admissibility with ABPN.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABPN requires general psychiatry certification by December 31 before the exam and one year of ACGME-accredited Addiction Psychiatry fellowship after psychiatry residency, subject to ABPN rules. The ABPN states it does not issue standalone board-eligibility statements; it determines exam admissibility on an active approved application. As of 2026-10-07, the 2026 exam deadlines were past and the page listed 2028 as the next choice of dates. This self-study conveys no eligibility. Verify rules/dates directly.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham; training sites at Massachusetts General Hospital, McLean Hospital, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and North Charles Foundation
officialProgrammes.name: Addiction Psychiatry Fellowship — one-year, full-time clinical track
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MGB page says ACGME-accredited since 1999 and usually taken during PGY-5 after ACGME Psychiatry residency. Public page lists rotations, didactics, modalities and sites, not a complete syllabus.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass General Brigham; same programme, clinical and research sites
officialProgrammes.name: Addiction Psychiatry Fellowship — two-year, half-time option (most often half-time clinical plus half-time research)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The public page describes a half-time option, usually research with an HMS mentor; it is an option of the same programme, not a separate institutional programme. Confirm ABPN continuity/minimum-time details with the board/director.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Supplied packet identifies one MGB clinical physician fellowship. Its official page is the primary source for programme claims, but its stated accreditation was not independently confirmed through ACGME ADS. Current ACGME 2026 requirements are linked. MGH Addiction Medicine and ABPM Addiction Medicine are separate. The McLean Norman E. Zinberg Addiction Psychiatry Research Fellowship is research support, not the ACGME clinical fellowship. No Johns Hopkins programme variant was in the supplied packet; this task does not assert an exhaustive directory search.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review; clinical contents are educational and must be checked against current sources and local protocols.
MGB self-reports accreditation; current ACGME ADS status not independently queried.
ABPN 2026 blueprint was posted March 2026; verify exam cycle and admission requirements directly.
MGB half-time track eligibility requires individualized board/director confirmation.
Research fellowships, Addiction Medicine and public directories are not equated with Addiction Psychiatry clinical training.
MUSC lists recordings as no-charge viewing. Vimeo oEmbed duration/date/title metadata was observed; direct automated page hit anti-bot; human playback should be verified.
Only seven unique Vimeo IDs are counted; no trailers, short PSAs, registered CME events, unknown durations, estimates, repeats or planned media.
Case authenticity/de-identification/reuse is not guaranteed. Never copy images, protected details or patient records.
Independent self-study grants no affiliation, accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, procedure competence, certification or guarantee of passing.

topicGaps: Verified free, observed-duration external runtime is 7.5469 h (27169 s), leaving 28.4531 h below the 36 h floor. The newly appended NIDA video is a single 33:27 COVID-era opioid-safety interview; original episode scripts are not recordings and do not close the runtime gap.

Unfilled or insufficiently taught board-relevant lecture topics remain: alcohol withdrawal/medications; core OUD care; sedatives; caffeine; inhalants; hallucinogens; PCP; gambling; forensic issues; diagnostic testing; family/group psychotherapy; law/ethics/access/QI. Six complete episode scripts (one introductory and five worked examples) add source-backed instruction in formulation, toxicology, alcohol-withdrawal continuity, MOUD reasoning, stimulant care, and benzodiazepine risk, but do not fully close these topic gaps.
Original teaching episodes in the separate authored file are scripted/planned only, not rendered or recorded. Their narration targets do not count toward verified media hours.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: Within what time window are DSM-5 SUD criteria counted, and what is the minimum criterion count?

options.text: At least 2 of 11 criteria within the same 12 months; severity is 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, 6+ severe. A lab alone does not diagnose.
Any positive toxicology result establishes a disorder, even without symptoms.
Tolerance alone establishes severe SUD.
The criteria are counted across the lifetime, with no required time window.

practiceQuestions.rationale: At least 2 of 11 criteria within the same 12 months; severity is 2–3 mild, 4–5 moderate, 6+ severe. A lab alone does not diagnose.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient is ambivalent about alcohol reduction. What response reflects motivational interviewing?

options.text: Confront denial and require a commitment to abstinence before offering help.
Ask permission to explore what matters and reflect concern plus uncertainty; avoid confrontation or an abstinence ultimatum.
Defer discussion until the patient independently requests treatment.
Tell the patient which goal to choose and end the conversation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ask permission to explore what matters and reflect concern plus uncertainty; avoid confrontation or an abstinence ultimatum.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the most accurate broad account of methadone/buprenorphine OUD treatment?

options.text: Methadone and buprenorphine are not opioid medications and cannot cause physical dependence.
Medication treatment is only useful during short detoxification and has no ongoing role.
FDA-approved medicines can reduce cravings/withdrawal and are associated with reduced overdose risk; individualize choice and discuss physiologic dependence without stigma.
Naltrexone activates the opioid receptor in the same way as methadone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FDA-approved medicines can reduce cravings/withdrawal and are associated with reduced overdose risk; individualize choice and discuss physiologic dependence without stigma.

practiceQuestions.stem: What issue should be addressed before starting naltrexone for a person with ongoing opioid exposure?

options.text: Naltrexone is a partial agonist, so ongoing opioid use does not affect initiation.
A single negative urine screen is sufficient to establish readiness in every case.
Naltrexone is the preferred medication to relieve acute opioid withdrawal.
As an antagonist, starting before adequate opioid abstinence may precipitate withdrawal; assess status and timing clinically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: As an antagonist, starting before adequate opioid abstinence may precipitate withdrawal; assess status and timing clinically.

practiceQuestions.stem: What follows alcohol withdrawal management?

options.text: Completion of withdrawal management alone is a complete AUD treatment.
It is one component of initiating/engaging in ongoing AUD treatment and recovery support, not standalone AUD treatment.
All patients require the same setting and medication plan.
AUD treatment should wait until every medical comorbidity has resolved.

practiceQuestions.rationale: It is one component of initiating/engaging in ongoing AUD treatment and recovery support, not standalone AUD treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with stimulant use has chest pain, agitation and hyperthermia. What comes first?

options.text: Wait for toxicology confirmation before assessing medical risk.
Begin an abstinence contract before examining the patient.
Identify urgent/emergent biomedical or psychiatric signs and arrange appropriate-level evaluation before longitudinal formulation.
Assume symptoms are a primary psychotic disorder without assessing intoxication or medical causes.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Identify urgent/emergent biomedical and psychiatric signs and arrange appropriate-level evaluation before longitudinal formulation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which behavioral treatment does the 2024 ASAM/AAAP guideline place as primary for stimulant use disorder?

options.text: No behavioral treatment is supported; medication is always first-line.
Contingency management should only be considered after years of treatment failure.
Involuntary residential admission is required for every patient.
Contingency management as a primary component, combined with appropriate psychosocial approaches such as CBT/CRA.

title: Musculoskeletal Oncology Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate physician-level independent study for orthopaedic surgeons, orthopaedic residents/fellows and interdisciplinary oncology clinicians; foundational orthopaedic anatomy, pathology, imaging, oncology and research literacy assumed. Public readings may also serve supervised learners.
prerequisites.requiredBeforeEnrollment: No admission or credential gate is asserted. This self-study does not assess eligibility for the real clinical fellowship. Clinical interventions belong only to licensed clinicians working within supervised accredited training and local policy.
assumedKnowledge: Basic radiology/pathology concepts and clinical reasoning
Fundamentals of cancer staging and evidence-based medicine
prerequisites.sequence: Take units 1–4 before disease blocks, then 5–10, then 11–12; review current authoritative disease-specific PDQ before any clinical application.

objectives: Describe an evidence-grounded multidisciplinary approach to suspected musculoskeletal neoplasia.
Construct a safe work-up and referral plan, with imaging and biopsy planning coordinated by the definitive sarcoma team.
Interpret radiologic and pathologic concepts as probabilistic inputs; communicate differential diagnoses and uncertainty.
Compare broad management principles for primary bone tumors, soft-tissue sarcomas, metastases, hematologic lesions and selected benign/intermediate lesions.
Discuss reconstruction, function, complications, survivorship, safety, ethics and research at a conceptual level without claiming procedural competence.
Navigate the distinction among an institutional fellowship, ACGME programme requirements, MSTS programme recognition and ABOS certification.

units.title: Foundations: orthopaedic oncology practice and tumor biology
objectives: Distinguish primary bone/soft-tissue neoplasms from metastasis, hematologic disease, infection, and pseudotumor in a structured differential.
Use age, compartment, anatomic site, bone segment, matrix, margins, and growth pattern to frame—not finalize—a differential.
Explain why multidisciplinary review and specialist referral precede definitive intervention for suspected sarcoma.
topics: Tumor biology; age/site/compartment reasoning; broad WHO-oriented classification; clinical history and examination; family-centered communication; referral thresholds.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: anatomy/pathophysiology; Patient Care: differential formulation; Communication; Professionalism
units.casePractice: Fictional vignette differential and referral memo; no diagnosis from a single sign/image.
units.assessment: One-page differential grid scored for breadth, uncertainty, and a defensible referral rationale.

units.title: Initial work-up, staging and biopsy planning
objectives: Build a pre-biopsy diagnostic/staging checklist for a suspected primary bone or soft-tissue sarcoma.
Explain why imaging and multidisciplinary coordination should precede biopsy and why the biopsy tract must be planned with the definitive team.
Identify referral and communication steps when an unplanned excision or outside biopsy has already occurred.
topics: History/exam; radiographs then cross-sectional imaging; whole-bone MRI for primary bone tumor extent; chest staging; biopsy method and tract concepts; specimen allocation; avoiding casual excision.
boardDomains: Patient Care: evaluation; Systems-Based Practice: coordination; Patient Safety; Communication
units.casePractice: Construct a staged work-up and explain biopsy coordination on a fictional referral.
units.assessment: Checklist rubric: sequence, appropriate staging, biopsy coordination, scope limits, escalation.

units.title: Imaging: radiograph, MRI, CT and systemic staging
objectives: Describe lesion location, margins, transition zone, matrix, cortical behavior, periosteal response and soft-tissue extension without treating any sign as pathognomonic.
Select imaging questions for radiography, MRI, CT and chest staging in a case conference format.
Recognize imaging limits and state when radiology/pathology correlation is required.
topics: Radiographs; entire involved bone and adjacent joint MRI; local CT for matrix/cortex when relevant; chest CT for pulmonary metastases; selected PET/bone imaging by disease pathway; structured report.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: imaging reasoning; Patient Care: safe staging; Interprofessional Communication
units.casePractice: Interpret authorized TCIA-linked de-identified dataset cases or screenshots viewed only on the source, describing findings and uncertainty.
units.assessment: Imaging presentation rubric: systematic description, appropriate next question, differential, staging limits.

units.title: Pathology, molecular classification and radiology-pathology concordance
objectives: Explain how histologic morphology and molecular findings contribute to modern sarcoma classification.
Identify core concepts that distinguish osteoid-producing malignant bone tumor, small-round-cell sarcoma, cartilage-forming tumor, and myxoid/adipocytic or spindle-cell soft-tissue sarcoma.
List triggers for specialist pathology review and additional testing without overreading a limited sample.
topics: Biopsy adequacy; representative sampling; malignant osteoid concept; immunohistochemistry and molecular testing as indicated; sampling heterogeneity; WHO classification changes; tumor board concordance.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: pathology and therapeutics; Patient Care: differential; Practice-Based Learning
units.casePractice: Prepare a fictional multidisciplinary pathology-radiology discrepancy note using published classification sources.
units.assessment: Rubric scores recognition of uncertainty, need for expert review, and restraint from single-marker diagnosis.

units.title: Primary malignant bone tumors: osteosarcoma and UPS of bone
objectives: Summarize risk-stratified evaluation and multidisciplinary treatment principles for localized, metastatic, and recurrent osteosarcoma.
Relate local staging, chest evaluation, tumor biology, and surgical local control to treatment planning.
Identify age, site, and histologic context that should prompt tailored review.
topics: Conventional and surface variants; staging; systemic therapy and surgery in coordinated protocols; margins/reconstruction concepts; metastases/recurrence; UPS of bone; survivorship/toxicities at a conceptual level.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: complex bone tumor; Patient Care: planning and complications; Systems-Based Practice
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional osteosarcoma pathways using current PDQ, explicitly avoiding regimen/dose prescriptions.
units.assessment: Treatment-board brief graded on sequencing, multidisciplinary roles, evidence/date checks, and caveats.

units.title: Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, chordoma and hematologic bone tumors
objectives: Compare the different treatment logic of Ewing sarcoma, chondrosarcoma, chordoma, lymphoma and myeloma involving bone.
Use the current disease-specific reference to identify when chemotherapy, radiation, or surgical local control is a multidisciplinary decision.
Avoid applying one bone-sarcoma pathway indiscriminately across histologies.
topics: Ewing molecular-pathologic framework and multimodal therapy; cartilage tumor grading and site; axial chordoma; lymphoma/myeloma as distinct disease families; referral/case conference.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: anatomy/pathophysiology/therapeutics; Patient Care: complex differential; Communication
units.casePractice: Create a comparison map from authoritative sources for four histologic categories.
units.assessment: Assessment checks histology-specific distinction and avoids unsupported treatment generalization.

units.title: Benign and intermediate bone lesions
objectives: Build a risk-aware differential for common benign and intermediate bone lesions using anatomy, age, growth, symptoms and imaging features.
Distinguish surveillance, additional work-up, biopsy and treatment as clinician/team decisions rather than automatic reactions to a label.
Explain recurrence, structural integrity and treatment-related morbidity as decision variables.
topics: Cartilage lesions; osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma; giant-cell tumor; bone cysts; fibrous lesions; Langerhans-cell histiocytosis; metabolic mimics; denosumab as a specialist-directed option.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: complex conditions; Patient Care: routine/complex procedure planning concepts; Systems-Based Practice
units.casePractice: Structured differential for a fictional lesion; require source corroboration and explain what data are still needed.
units.assessment: Rubric: reasoning, escalation/surveillance rationale, avoid overcalling benignity, patient-centered trade-offs.

units.title: Malignant soft-tissue sarcoma
objectives: Organize the differential and work-up for a deep or enlarging soft-tissue mass and explain specialist referral.
Summarize multimodal local control and systemic therapy as histology/site/stage-dependent team decisions.
Discuss the consequences of an unplanned excision and the importance of margin and radiotherapy planning.
topics: Extremity/trunk/retroperitoneal/head-neck context; MRI; planned biopsy; grade and histology; surgery; pre/postoperative radiotherapy trade-offs; systemic therapy; recurrence and metastatic disease.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: complex soft-tissue tumors; Patient Care: planning; Communication; Systems-Based Practice
units.casePractice: Write a fictional referral-team case conference summary without specifying a patient treatment order.
units.assessment: Rubric: staging, teamwork, local-control reasoning, uncertainty and citation currency.

units.title: Benign soft-tissue, nerve and synovial lesions
objectives: Use anatomy, depth, symptoms, growth and imaging/pathology concordance to structure evaluation of common benign soft-tissue masses.
Recognize that benign-appearing labels do not supersede red flags or discordance.
Explain how multidisciplinary input can reduce avoidable harm from an inappropriate excision.
topics: Lipomatous, vascular, neural, fibrous, synovial lesions; peripheral nerve tumor differential; imaging/pathology concordance; symptom/functional assessment; follow-up questions.
boardDomains: Medical Knowledge: differential; Patient Care: safe evaluation; Professionalism
units.casePractice: Case worksheet using a source-linked TCIA cohort only if applicable; constructed scenario remains labeled fictional.
units.assessment: Grading: differential quality, escalation criteria, uncertainty and communication.

units.title: Skeletal metastases, myeloma and metabolic bone disease
objectives: Differentiate the orthopaedic-oncology question in skeletal metastasis from the primary sarcoma work-up.
Describe how site, lesion extent, symptoms, prognosis and anticipated mechanical failure are considered by the multidisciplinary team.
Identify hematologic and metabolic mimics and communicate a safe escalation plan.
topics: Metastatic carcinoma; myeloma/lymphoma; pathologic fracture context; stabilization/reconstruction principles; palliative goals; metabolic mimics; radiation/systemic oncology coordination.
boardDomains: Patient Care: complex musculoskeletal condition; Systems-Based Practice; Professionalism
units.casePractice: Fictional proximal femur lesion discussion with uncertainty and a question list for tumor board.
units.assessment: Rubric: team coordination, safety, prognosis caveats and no unsupported procedural decision.

units.title: Surgical planning, reconstruction, complications and function
objectives: Compare conceptual goals and trade-offs among limb-salvage, amputation, endoprosthetic/allograft reconstruction and selected complex-site reconstruction.
Describe how neurovascular anatomy, soft-tissue coverage, growth, function and complication contingencies shape team plans.
Identify complications and formulate high-level safety/rehabilitation communication without claiming operative competence.
topics: Preoperative indications conference; margins and reconstruction options; pelvis/spine/axial disease; allograft/endoprosthesis; amputation/rotationplasty; rehabilitation; infection, failure, recurrence and reoperation.
boardDomains: ACGME Patient Care: operative planning/case-log domains; Medical Knowledge; Systems-Based Practice; Communication
units.casePractice: Create a fictional multidisciplinary decision matrix; no procedural step-by-step training or patient-specific advice.
units.assessment: Rubric: options, harms/benefits, team input, functional priorities, complication contingencies.

units.title: Longitudinal care, ethics, evidence appraisal and improvement
objectives: Plan a high-level survivorship and follow-up discussion that includes late effects, function, psychosocial needs and transition of care.
Critically appraise clinical study design, endpoints, evidence certainty and external validity in rare tumors.
Apply patient safety, professionalism, consent, privacy and quality-improvement principles to educational cases.
topics: Late effects and survivorship; care transitions; shared decision making; clinical research/IRB; rare disease evidence; QI; safety reporting; confidentiality; disability and family-centered care.
boardDomains: ACGME Professionalism; Practice-Based Learning; Systems-Based Practice; Communication; Patient Care
units.casePractice: Two-page appraisal of a peer-reviewed study and a fictional handoff/safety reflection.
units.assessment: Final assessment rubric: methods 25%, evidence interpretation 25%, safe team plan 25%, ethics/communication 25%.

assignment.title: Fictional sarcoma tumor-board dossier
assignment.description: Across a clearly marked fictional adult or pediatric scenario, prepare a 1,500–2,000 word structured dossier: initial differential; information still needed; staging/work-up sequence; referral/biopsy coordination considerations; radiology-pathology questions; multidisciplinary management options and trade-offs; patient/family communication; source-date check; and a short evidence-appraisal note. Use only linked public sources or lawful TCIA datasets under their terms. Do not include real patient records, images copied from repositories, actual clinical recommendations for an identifiable person, drug doses, or operative instructions.

rubric.standard: Differential is defensible; alternatives, uncertainty, missing data and escalation are explicit.
Imaging/staging sequence is sourced; biopsy coordination/referral and safety are addressed.
Roles and high-level options/harms are balanced, not prescriptive.
Uses current authoritative references and labels programme, board and accreditation statements correctly.
Case fictional/deidentified; privacy, access, patient/family communication and no-scope caveat present.

assessment.format: 10 original multiple-choice questions plus unit-level case-analysis assignments, a formative image description, and final fictional tumor-board dossier; these are educational checks, not validated board items or a predictor of board passing.
assessment.passStandard: No pass standard implying clinical competence or certification. Learners should review rationales and unresolved topics with qualified faculty in their accredited programme.
assessment.domains: ACGME musculoskeletal-oncology milestones are developmental fellowship assessment tools, not a public ABOS exam blueprint. ABOS primary orthopaedics exams are separate. No orthopaedic-oncology-specific board exam was identified.

topicGaps: Verified recordings cover only 2.4922 of the 36 target hours; the remaining 33.5078 hours are not verified and no planned/scripted teaching counts toward them.

Most fellowship-level material remains uncovered by runtime-verified free recordings: pathology/molecular classification, imaging and biopsy planning beyond one general recording, disease-specific contemporary care across bone and soft-tissue histologies, hematologic bone disease, metastasis decision frameworks, complex axial reconstruction, survivorship, complications, ethics and research appraisal.

The added pediatric POSNA clips are short reconstruction segments (38:48 total across the three relevant clips); they do not supply full clinical training, a comprehensive pediatric tumor curriculum, or procedural competence.

Public institutional curriculum blocks and ACGME requirements establish themes and training standards, not a publicly verified MGB lecture archive or measured didactic hours. The MSTS webinar archive did not expose exact playable durations for most listed items at review; those were not counted.

Original authored episodes are scripts only, not rendered or clinically reviewed; remaining-hour feasibility depends on locating/clearing and runtime-verifying roughly 33.5 additional hours of relevant accessible lectures or producing and reviewing substantial new media.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The supplied official packet lists Mass General Brigham. Official MGB/MGH public pages describe the exact institutional clinical fellowship as Massachusetts General Hospital Orthopaedic Oncology Fellowship and name Boston Children’s Hospital as the joint base. MSTS uses “Mass General/Brigham (Harvard)” and publishes a current status row. These are name/host variants of one MGB/MGH/BCH clinical physician fellowship, not separate specialties. No Johns Hopkins variant is established by the supplied packet or sources reviewed. MGB public page does not disclose a full rotation schedule or the complete teaching media; no case volumes are inferred.
sourceCaveats: Programme pages are current institutional descriptions, not independent certification records or complete internal curricula. Public sources do not disclose complete clinical rotations, lectures, case volumes, supervision records or training outcomes.

The MSTS directory currently marks MGB/Mass General-Brigham ACGME Yes / MSTS No, while its fellowship guidelines say ACGME-accredited programmes are automatically recognized. The public sources conflict; status needs direct confirmation.

ABOS public subspecialty list includes only Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine certificates. No separate ABOS orthopaedic-oncology examination is described; do not infer from this course any board pathway beyond the official primary ABOS requirements.

One YouTube lecture has a displayed runtime verified at 1:06:59; exact metadata extraction for other public candidate videos failed or did not surface a duration, so they are excluded from verified hours. Older video claims may be dated or inaccurate.

Current clinical decisions must be made by qualified multidisciplinary clinicians using current guidelines and the patient’s actual context. Human clinical review of this curriculum has not been performed.

topicGaps: Verified recordings cover only 2.4922 of the 36 target hours; the remaining 33.5078 hours are not verified and no planned/scripted teaching counts toward them.

Most fellowship-level material remains uncovered by runtime-verified free recordings: pathology/molecular classification, imaging and biopsy planning beyond one general recording, disease-specific contemporary care across bone and soft-tissue histologies, hematologic bone disease, metastasis decision frameworks, complex axial reconstruction, survivorship, complications, ethics and research appraisal.

The added pediatric POSNA clips are short reconstruction segments (38:48 total across the three relevant clips); they do not supply full clinical training, a comprehensive pediatric tumor curriculum, or procedural competence.

Public institutional curriculum blocks and ACGME requirements establish themes and training standards, not a publicly verified MGB lecture archive or measured didactic hours. The MSTS webinar archive did not expose exact playable durations for most listed items at review; those were not counted.

Original authored episodes are scripts only, not rendered or clinically reviewed; remaining-hour feasibility depends on locating/clearing and runtime-verifying roughly 33.5 additional hours of relevant accessible lectures or producing and reviewing substantial new media.
